> As a proxy for the existence of such distinctive features, a separate group of participants provided ratings of the extent to which each rock image possessed a highly distinctive feature not present in other items in the set.

> Also following Nosofsky et al. ( 2025), for simplicity in the analysis, we assumed that all participants were governed by the same parameter values, i.e., we did not attempt to account for individualparticipant differences.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

ownership.dep_description: Most of the major trends in recognition-memory data from studies using words and pictures can be predicted with a small number of core processes, suggesting these processes are fundamentally important. The case for this assertion is supported by results and modeling of three long-term recognition memory studies, using a new design, and showing the core processes generalize well between different task types, list lengths and stimulus types. In most conditions memory was tested with two items: both or neither from the list, or one from the list. In Experiment 1, in two-alternative forced choice blocks the more likely old item was to be chosen; in four-way classification blocks the two items were to be classified as both old, both new, or one old and one new. Experiment 2 required judgment of the item more likely new. Experiment 3 added blocks of single item old-new testing. The 288 distinct conditions giving probabilities of correct and error responses were predicted very accurately b...

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 20 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: As a proxy for the existence of such distinctive features, a separate group of participants provided ratings of the extent to which each rock image possessed a highly distinctive feature not present in other items in the set.

Also following Nosofsky et al. ( 2025), for simplicity in the analysis, we assumed that all participants were governed by the same parameter values, i.e., we did not attempt to account for individualparticipant differences.

info.title: An MDS-REM Model for Predicting Individual-Item Perceptual Old-New Recognition

author.affiliation:
Psychological and Brain Sciences
								Indiana University
								
									Bloomington 2

Melbourne School of Psychological Sciences
								The University of Melbourne

text.text: The Retrieving Effectively from Memory (REM) model (Shiffrin & Stevyers, 1997)  is an extremely influential model of old-new recognition memory based on Bayesian reasoning principles that provides a comprehensive account of diverse memory phenomena.
text.formatted: The Retrieving Effectively from Memory (REM) model (Shiffrin & Stevyers, 1997)  is an extremely influential model of old-new recognition memory based on Bayesian reasoning principles that provides a comprehensive account of diverse memory phenomena.

text.text: However, a limitation of extant versions of the model is that it does not provide accounts of recognition memory at the level of individual items based on their precise positions in multidimensional similarity space and their possession of item-specific distinctive features.

Instead, it assumes a geometric probability distribution for generating hypothetical features and relies on computer simulation to generate predictions of patterns of results for large classes of items and experimental manipulations.

Here we move in the direction of filling that gap by proposing a REM-like model in which individual items are represented in one-to-one correspondence as points in multidimensional similarity (MDS) spaces and in which information regarding distinctive features possessed by individual objects is also provided.

Rather than using the geometric-probability distribution assumed by Shiffrin and Steyvers, this "MDS-REM" model uses continuous probability density functions defined over the continuous-dimension MDS spaces.

The model is tested using data sets from three previously reported perceptual old-new recognition studies and provides reasonably accurate predictions of performance at the level of individual items or categories, including accounts of how both false-alarm and hit rates are influenced by detailed similarity relations among items and their possession of item-specific distinctive features.
A central topic addressed in the cognitive-psychology of episodic memory is how observers make recognition judgments of whether items are "old" (previously experienced) or "new".

Among the major computational models of old-new recognition memory are members of the class of "global-familiarity" models (Gillund & Shiffrin, 1984; Hintzman, 1988; Kahana & Sekuler, 2002; Murdock, 1982; Nosofsky, 1988 Nosofsky, , 1991;; Osth, Zhang, & Williams, 2025; Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997; for reviews, see Clark & Gronlund, 1996; Osth & Dennis, 2024).
text.formatted: Among the major computational models of old-new recognition memory are members of the class of "global-familiarity" models <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Gillund & Shiffrin, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Hintzman, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Kahana & Sekuler, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Murdock, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Nosofsky, 1988</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Nosofsky, , 1991;;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Osth, Zhang, & Williams, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997</ref>; for reviews, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Clark & Gronlund, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Osth & Dennis, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: According to this class of models, presentation of a test item leads to a global-activation of the contents of memory based on how similar the test item is to the underlying memory representations.
The greater the global activation, the more familiar the item seems, and the greater is the probability that the observer judges the item to be old.

Although prominent models have also been proposed that posit that there are multiple processes underlying old-new recognition (e.g., Malmberg, Holden, & Shiffrin, 2004; Wixted, 2007; Yonelinas, 2002), the focus in this article is on the single-process global-familiarity class.
text.formatted: Although prominent models have also been proposed that posit that there are multiple processes underlying old-new recognition (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Malmberg, Holden, & Shiffrin, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Wixted, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Yonelinas, 2002)</ref>, the focus in this article is on the single-process global-familiarity class.

text.text: Our specific focus in this article is on a member of the class of global-familiarity models proposed by Shiffrin and Steyvers (1997) known as REM (Retrieving Effectively from Memory).
text.formatted: Our specific focus in this article is on a member of the class of global-familiarity models proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Shiffrin and Steyvers (1997)</ref> known as REM (Retrieving Effectively from Memory).

text.text: We describe the detailed computational ideas in REM below.

The general idea, however, is that by making a global comparison of a test item to the contents of memory, the memory system computes the likelihood that the test item is "old" and the likelihood that the test item is "new" and forms a ratio of these likelihoods.

If the likelihood ratio exceeds a criterion value -which has an ideal-observer value equal to 1, reflecting an equal likelihood that the item is old or new -then the system responds "old", else the system responds "new".

The original version of REM as well as significant extensions of the model (Cox & Shiffrin, 2017; Criss, 2006; Criss, Malmberg, & Shiffrin, 2011; Mohamed, Meyer-Grant, & Shiffrin, 2026) have proven successful at accounting for an enormous collection of fundamental results from the old-new recognition literature, including the list-length effect, the null liststrength effect, the mirror effect, the shape of ROC curves, word-frequency effects, effects of presentation time and signal-to-respond methods, memory for pictures versus words, effects of "oldness" vs. "newness" judgments in wide varieties of forced-choice recognition tasks, and numerous other fundamental results.

text.text: This coverage is impressive when one considers that many of these results were challenging for previous models to explain (Glanzer & Adams, 1990; Ratcliff, Sheu, & Gronlund, 1992; Shiffrin, Ratcliff, & Clark, 1990).

text.text: However, a limitation of extant versions of the model is they are not designed to predict the probability with which observers recognize individual items as being old or new based on the items' precise locations in a multidimensional similarity space.
The reason is that extant versions of REM do not identify specific multidimensional representations corresponding to specific items tested in experiments.
Instead, applications of the model use simulation techniques in which features of hypothetical items are generated by using a geometric-probability distribution.

This approach is used for representing general "classes" of items, such as low-frequency or highfrequency words and pictures, but the modeling approach does not develop individualized representations corresponding in one-to-one fashion to the individual items themselves.

This is an obvious downside when one considers that the prediction of individual-item identification and old-new recognition based on the positions of items in multidimensional similarity space has been a classic goal in past tests of cognitive-process models of memory (e.g., Nosofsky, 1988 Nosofsky, , 1991 Nosofsky, , 1992;; Shepard, 1957 Shepard, , 1958)).
text.formatted: This is an obvious downside when one considers that the prediction of individual-item identification and old-new recognition based on the positions of items in multidimensional similarity space has been a classic goal in past tests of cognitive-process models of memory (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Nosofsky, 1988</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Nosofsky, , 1991</ref> <ref type="bibr">Nosofsky, , 1992;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Shepard, 1957</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Shepard, , 1958))</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, this goal is an emerging direction in modern computational modeling work aimed at predicting individual-item recognition for items drawn from high-dimensional, real-world perceptual and semantic domains (e.g., Chang, Johns, & Brainerd, 2025; Meagher & Nosofsky, 2023; Nosofsky, Ehinger, & Osth, 2025; Osth, Zhang, & Williams, 2026; Reid & Jamieson, 2023).

text.text: Much of this modern computational modeling work is motivated by the recent literature on "memorability" that seeks to understand why certain realworld individual items are recognized with high accuracy and others are more easily forgotten (Bainbridge, 2019; Kramer, Hebart, et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Much of this modern computational modeling work is motivated by the recent literature on "memorability" that seeks to understand why certain realworld individual items are recognized with high accuracy and others are more easily forgotten <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bainbridge, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Kramer, Hebart, et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: We discuss this literature in more detail in our General Discussion.
Thus, the central purpose of the present work was to move in the direction of adapting REM to allow it to make such individual-item predictions.
Before proceeding, we should note that this goal was pursued long ago by Mark Steyvers in his 2000 Ph.D. dissertation in the domain of word recognition (Steyvers, 2000).
text.formatted: Before proceeding, we should note that this goal was pursued long ago by Mark Steyvers in his 2000 Ph.D. dissertation in the domain of word recognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Steyvers, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Using a large database of free association norms, Steyvers located individual words in word-association spaces and combined these representations with REM to predict a variety of qualitative effects in word-recognition experiments.

However, although his approach yielded predictions of individual-word hit and false-alarm rates that improved upon models that represent words with arbitrary features, he characterized the achieved correlations as "moderate".

In the present work, we propose a REMlike model intended to capture results at the level of individual items in domains of perceptual old-new recognition rather than word recognition and use alternative methods for locating the items in multidimensional similarity spaces.
At the outset, we need to emphasize that the original version of REM was developed in the form of an ideal-observer model derived from a Bayesian likelihood-ratio framework.

To derive the model, Shiffrin and Steyvers (1997) assumed a probabilistic world in which the features that composed old study items and new lures were generated from an identical geometric-probability distribution.
text.formatted: To derive the model, <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Shiffrin and Steyvers (1997)</ref> assumed a probabilistic world in which the features that composed old study items and new lures were generated from an identical geometric-probability distribution.

text.text: The study items were presumed to be stored in noisy fashion in memory.

Given their specific assumptions, Shiffrin and Steyvers developed precise idealobserver equations for computing the likelihoods that test items were old or new (for details, see Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997, pp. 147, 163) and the model would respond that the test item was "old" if the computed likelihood-ratio exceeded a criterion (often set to an optimal value of 1).
text.formatted: Given their specific assumptions, Shiffrin and Steyvers developed precise idealobserver equations for computing the likelihoods that test items were old or new (for details, see <ref type="bibr">Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997, pp. 147, 163)</ref> and the model would respond that the test item was "old" if the computed likelihood-ratio exceeded a criterion (often set to an optimal value of 1).

text.text: As explained above, however, any simulated item that was stored in memory was intended to serve only as a representative from a general class of items -the simulated memory representation did not correspond to any specific item tested in the behavioral experiments.

In the present work, we retain core ideas motivated by original REM but no longer operate in the probabilistic world defined by the geometric probability distribution that was assumed by Shiffrin and Steyvers. Instead, because our goal will be to develop a REM-like model capable of predicting old-new recognition probabilities for individual items lying in continuous-dimension similarity spaces, we will make use of continuous probability functions defined in those spaces.
text.formatted: In the present work, we retain core ideas motivated by original REM but no longer operate in the probabilistic world defined by the geometric probability distribution that was assumed by <ref type="bibr">Shiffrin and Steyvers.</ref> Instead, because our goal will be to develop a REM-like model capable of predicting old-new recognition probabilities for individual items lying in continuous-dimension similarity spaces, we will make use of continuous probability functions defined in those spaces.

text.text: Although the model will retain many of the core conceptual ideas from original REM, we make no claims that the version that we develop and test is an ideal-observer model.
Our REM-like alternative differs from original REM in another important way.

In the original REM model, the researchers simulated probabilistic memory representations for study items that differed from one simulation to the next and then applied a deterministic decision rule for making old-new recognition judgments in any given simulation.
The predictions of old-new judgments were probabilistic because of noisy storage of the study items across the multiple simulations.

This use of simulation techniques made quantitative parameter-estimation difficult, so the researchers often reported parameter settings that yielded good qualitative accounts of the overall patterns of results without necessarily achieving optimal quantitative fits.

By comparison, here we will be interested in using our REM-like model for generating precise quantitative predictions at the level of individual items, which will require challenging and computationally expensive parameter searches.

To make this goal more tractable, we will assume for simplicity that the observer stores error-free versions of the study items in memory and we will place the "noise" in observers' judgments within a probabilistic decision rule rather than using a deterministic one.
An advantage of implementing the model in this manner is that it can be expressed in analytic form without the need for use of computer simulation.
Our proposed REM-like model borrows ideas from another global-familiarity model of old-new recognition, namely the hybrid-similarity generalized context model (GCM) of Nosofsky and Zaki (2003).
text.formatted: Our proposed REM-like model borrows ideas from another global-familiarity model of old-new recognition, namely the hybrid-similarity generalized context model (GCM) of <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Nosofsky and Zaki (2003)</ref>.

text.text: That model has proven successful at predicting varieties of old-new recognition at the level of individual items, including recent applications in high-dimensional real-world domains (Meagher & Nosofsky, 2023; Nosofsky, Ehinger, & Osth, 2025).
text.formatted: That model has proven successful at predicting varieties of old-new recognition at the level of individual items, including recent applications in high-dimensional real-world domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Meagher & Nosofsky, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Nosofsky, Ehinger, & Osth, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, before transitioning to our proposed adaptation of REM, we first briefly describe the gist of the hybrid-similarity GCM and an example experiment to which it has been applied.
This experiment will also serve as our first testing ground for our proposed adapted version of REM.

A core idea in the hybrid-similarity GCM is to use multidimensional-scaling (MDS) techniques to embed objects in continuous multidimensional similarity spaces (Lee, 2001; Shepard, 1958 Shepard, , 1980)).
text.formatted: A core idea in the hybrid-similarity GCM is to use multidimensional-scaling (MDS) techniques to embed objects in continuous multidimensional similarity spaces <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Lee, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Shepard, 1958</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Shepard, , 1980))</ref>.

text.text: These same MDS representations will be used in our proposed adaptation of REM; thus, for ease of description, we will term our proposed adaptation the MDS-REM model.

Beyond the use of the continuous-dimension MDS representation, however, the hybridsimilarity GCM also incorporates an independent set of ratings that measure the presence of "distinctive features" possessed by the objects.
As explained below, the distinctive features seem intuitively to "stand outside" of the derived continuous MDS spaces.

Extensive past research has demonstrated the fundamental importance of item distinctiveness in mediating old-new recognition and these distinctiveness ratings have played a fundamental role in allowing the hybrid-similarity GCM to account quantitatively for varieties of old-new recognition performance.
The MDS-REM model will make use of these distinctive-feature ratings as well.

Although the hybrid-similarity GCM and MDS-REM model both make use of the same MDS and distinctive-feature information in computing a global-familiarity signal across all stored memory traces, we will see some potentially important conceptual differences between the models in how they make use of the information.
Our focus here will be on the newly proposed MDS-REM model, but we provide a fuller discussion of the relation between the models in our General Discussion.

In a recent test of the hybrid-similarity GCM, Meagher and Nosofsky (2023) reported an experiment in which observers learned to classify a set of 180 rock-image stimuli into three geologically-defined superordinate categories (igneous, metamorphic and sedimentary).

text.text: (There were 6 training items sampled from each of 10 subtype categories composing each of the 3 superordinate categories, for a total of 180 training items.)
Following the training phase, observers engaged in a classification transfer-test phase involving the original 180 training items and 360 novel transfer stimuli.
In addition, during the transfer test, observers made recognition judgments of whether each of the 540 individual items was old or new.
In this article we focus on only the old-new recognition data.

Importantly, a subset of the novel transfer items had a special status of being "high-similarity neighbors" (HSNs): Meagher and Nosofsky (2023) used photoshopping techniques to construct a set of HSN lures that were highly similar to individual target items from the old training set (for illustrative examples, see Meagher & Nosofsky, 2023, Figure 1).

text.text: The expectation was that false-alarm rates for the HSN lures would be relatively high in magnitude.

In previous work, Nosofsky et al. (2018 Nosofsky et al. ( , 2020) ) and Meagher and Nosofsky (2023) had collected extensive similarity scaling data and conducted MDS analyses of the similarity data to embed the 540 rock images in a multidimensional similarity space.

( , 2020) )</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Meagher and Nosofsky (2023)</ref> had collected extensive similarity scaling data and conducted MDS analyses of the similarity data to embed the 540 rock images in a multidimensional similarity space.

text.text: Based on a combination of overall fit and interpretability of the derived dimensions, they settled on use of an 8-dimensional MDS solution for representing the individual images in the continuous-dimension space.

The dimensions of the space correlated strongly with attribute ratings (provided by independent groups of subjects) of lightness/darkness, average grain size, smoothness/roughness, shininess, chromaticity, organization, red/green hue, and shape-related components.
However, many of the rock images also had highly idiosyncratic distinctive features that seemed to go "outside" this continuous-dimension space.

For example, obsidian is a smooth, shiny, dark black glassy rock; however, one of the obsidian samples had a series of prominent bright red stripes across its surface that seemed to make it "stand out" from other rock images in the set.
Other examples include rocks with prominent embedded crystals or a rock with a prominent fossil embedded in it.

As a proxy for the existence of such distinctive features, a separate group of participants provided ratings of the extent to which each rock image possessed a highly distinctive feature not present in other items in the set.

(For examples of rock images that received high vs. low distinctive-feature ratings, see Fig. 12 of Meagher & Nosofsky, 2023.) Although these ratings provide partial information about presence of distinctive features, a limitation is that the method does not identify the actual specific distinctive features that are present in each item.

text.text: Before presenting the MDS-REM equations, we highlight a key conceptual issue involving the prediction of hit and false-alarm rates in old-new recognition that needs to be addressed by MDS-REM (and all members of the class of global-familiarity models).
In general, global-familiarity models predict higher probabilities of false alarms when lures are highly similar to the study items than when they have low similarity.
In such cases, summed interitem similarity (i.e., global-familiarity) will be high, so observers will have a higher probability of false-alarming to such lures.
The picture is not so clear regarding the prediction of hit rates for old targets.

On the one hand, if an old target is embedded in a dense region of the similarity space (i.e., if it is similar to many other old study items), then many traditional global-familiarity models (e.g., Gillund & Shiffrin, 1984; Hintzman, 1988; Nosofsky, 1991) would predict that it too would tend to have high summed interitem similarity, so presumably would generate a relatively high-magnitude familiarity signal.
text.formatted: On the one hand, if an old target is embedded in a dense region of the similarity space (i.e., if it is similar to many other old study items), then many traditional global-familiarity models (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Gillund & Shiffrin, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Hintzman, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Nosofsky, 1991)</ref> would predict that it too would tend to have high summed interitem similarity, so presumably would generate a relatively high-magnitude familiarity signal.

text.text: Using this line of reasoning, the expectation would be that targets located in dense regions of the similarity space should have relatively high hit rates.

Empirical evidence suggests, however, that exactly the opposite is true: it is often the case that highly distinctive old targets that lie in isolated, sparse regions of the similarity space have the highest hit rates.

For example, as brought out by Valentine and Ferrara (1991) and Busey and Tunnicluff (1999), faces with highly distinctive scars that lie in sparse regions of multidimensional similarity space often have higher hit rates than do more typical faces without such distinctive features.
text.formatted: For example, as brought out by <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Valentine and Ferrara (1991)</ref> and <ref type="bibr">Busey and Tunnicluff (1999)</ref>, faces with highly distinctive scars that lie in sparse regions of multidimensional similarity space often have higher hit rates than do more typical faces without such distinctive features.

text.text: In the hybrid-similarity GCM (Nosofsky & Zaki, 2003), the proposed explanation for this pattern of results is that targets with highly distinctive features have higher self-similarity to their own representations than do targets without such features.
text.formatted: In the hybrid-similarity GCM <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Nosofsky & Zaki, 2003)</ref>, the proposed explanation for this pattern of results is that targets with highly distinctive features have higher self-similarity to their own representations than do targets without such features.

text.text: This idea is directly motivated by Tversky's (1977) feature-contrast model of similarity, which predicts that the addition of salient features to an object will boost its self-similarity.
text.formatted: This idea is directly motivated by <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Tversky's (1977)</ref> feature-contrast model of similarity, which predicts that the addition of salient features to an object will boost its self-similarity.

text.text: If the boosted selfsimilarity is sufficiently high, then overall global summed similarity (which is a combination of self-similarity and summed interitem similarity) will also be very high, and observers will display high hit rates for items with highly distinctive features.

The hybrid-similarity GCM has provided reasonably good accounts of patterns of old-new recognition involving items with distinctive features in its previous tests (Azarov & Nosofsky, in press; Knapp, Nosofsky, & Busey, 2006; Meagher & Nosofsky, 2023; Nosofsky, Ehinger, & Osth, 2025; Nosofsky & Zaki, 2003), whereas the model fails to account for the data if the role of the distinctive features is not incorporated in its machinery.

text.text: As we will see, the version of MDS-REM that we propose has an alternative conceptual explanation for the reason why items with highly distinctive features often have high hit rates.
Nevertheless, incorporating information about the presence of the distinctive features will be critical to its operation as well.
We return to this crucial issue after providing our formal statement of our modified REM-like model.

Formal Statement of MDS-REM Shiffrin and Steyvers's (1997) original REM model assumes that individual items presented on a study list are represented as individual traces in memory; however, due to noise in encoding, some features either are not stored or are stored incorrectly.
text.formatted: Formal Statement of MDS-REM <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Shiffrin and Steyvers's (1997)</ref> original REM model assumes that individual items presented on a study list are represented as individual traces in memory; however, due to noise in encoding, some features either are not stored or are stored incorrectly.

text.text: Our newly proposed MDS-REM also assumes that each study item is represented as an individual memory trace; however, in our adapted version of the model, we assume for simplicity that all the complete memory traces are stored and that they are stored in an error-free manner.
In our situation, the study and test items are assumed to reside in a continuous multidimensional space with M dimensions.
The value of each item i on each dimension m is given by its coordinate value on dimension m (xim) in the MDS solution derived for the objects.
The original REM assumed that each item on a study list of size n has been presented one time on the study list and we adopt this simplifying assumption as well.
Each study item gives rise to an individualized memory trace.
Following Shiffrin and Steyvers (1997), the resulting set of n memory traces constitutes the "data" (D) and each individual memory trace is denoted by Dj.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Shiffrin and Steyvers (1997)</ref>, the resulting set of n memory traces constitutes the "data" (D) and each individual memory trace is denoted by Dj.

text.text: Because of our assumption of error-free storage, the values of each Dj along its M MDS dimensions are simply the coordinates of item j in the MDS solution.

Recall that the test items and memory traces are also presumed to possess distinctive features that go outside the continuous MDS solution, and these will be incorporated in the model's machinery as well (see below).

Following Shiffrin and Steyvers (1997), conditioned upon presentation of some test item i, the system computes: 1) the probability that the test item is "old" (O) given the complete collection of memory-trace data (D), P(O|D); and 2) the probability that the test item is "new" (N) given the complete collection of memory-trace data, P(N|D).

text.text: With regard to the continuous MDS coordinates that compose the traces, our proposal is that the system assumes that each memory trace is a multivariate normal distortion of whatever test probe i created it, with the mean of the multivariate normal being the coordinates of test probe i itself.
For simplicity, we assume that each dimension of the multivariate normal has the same standard deviation σs and that there is zero correlation between any pair of dimensions.

In the case in which the test probe i really does correspond to a specific memory trace j, the probe and memory trace will have identical values of the distinctive features (given our assumption of error-free storage), so the distinctive-feature component will not "subtract" from the probability density that memory trace j would be produced by test probe i.

[Assume further that we are not dealing with the special case described earlier in which the test probe is a high-similarity neighbor (HSN) of the study item that produced memory-trace j.]

Within the continuous MDS space, the probability-density P(Dj|Sj) is computed in the same manner as in Equation 3a, except now the values xim and xjm will be mismatching across the M dimensions, yielding a lower probability density that memory-trace j was produced by test probe i.

text.text: In addition, the test probe and the memory trace are now very unlikely to share the same distinctive features; we will assume for simplicity that their distinctive features do in fact differ from one another.
This mismatch on the distinctive features will further reduce the memory system's computation of P(Dj|Sj).

In the present paradigm, we do not know the actual identity of the distinctive features of each item, but the ratings of feature distinctiveness provided by the independent group of participants allows us to approximate the amount of reduction that is involved.

Let δi ' denote the mean distinctive feature rating that participants in the rating study provided to test probe i, and let δj ' denote the mean distinctive feature rating that participants in the rating study provided to item j.

Because the absolute magnitudes of the scale of distinctive feature ratings are arbitrary, we make allowance for a monotonic, nonlinear transformation of the raw mean ratings onto a psychological distinctiveness scale (for details, see Appendix A), producing transformed distinctive-feature ratings δi and δj.

(The parameter values αT and αM do not depend on which specific items serve as test probes versus memory traces; they are fixed scaling constants.)

Intuitively, for example, to the extent that test probe i has a highly distinctive feature not shared by memory trace j, the probability density that test probe i might have produced memory-trace j is reduced.
Likewise, if memory trace j includes a highly distinctive feature not shared by test probe i, then the probability density that probe i produced trace j is also reduced.

We make allowance for separate values of αT and αM because there may be differential, asymmetric influences of distinctive features of test probes and memory traces on the memory system's computations of the probability densities.
Note that the same Equation 4holds both for test probes that were study items but not ones that produced a particular memory-trace j and for standard lures presented during the test phase.
text.formatted: Note that the same Equation <ref type="formula" target="#formula_6">4</ref>holds both for test probes that were study items but not ones that produced a particular memory-trace j and for standard lures presented during the test phase.

text.text: For reasons already explained above, the values of P(Dj|Sj) yielded by such test probes will be considerably lower than the one yielded for a test probe that actually did produce memory-trace j.
Finally, for the present paradigm, a special case of P(Dj|Sj) to consider is one which the test probe is an HSN lure.
Consider in particular the case in which a specific memory-trace j was produced by the study item that is the "parent" of the HSN lure.

Unlike for standard lures, in this case the distinctive features of the HSN lure are likely to be quite similar to the distinctive features of this special-case memory trace (because they were both produced by the same parent).
Thus, in this special case, the memory system would reduce the probability density P(Dj|Sj) to a much smaller degree than for standard lures.

To capture this behavior of the memory system, the model assumes that, for the special case in which an HSN lure is being compared to the memory trace produced by its parent, the probability density with which the HSN lure would produce the parent-generated memory trace is given by where v is a fixed freely estimated scaling parameter that reduces the magnitude of the mismatch between the distinctive features of the HSN lure and its parent-generated memory trace.
1 For all other comparisons involving HSN lures, the previous Equation 4 applies for computing P(Dj|Sj).
For the reasons explained above, our expectation is that the estimate of v will be less than one.
The next step in the modeling is to set values for the P(Dj|Nj) probability densities that appear in the denominators of the individual-trace likelihood-ratio terms in Equation 2.
text.formatted: The next step in the modeling is to set values for the P(Dj|Nj) probability densities that appear in the denominators of the individual-trace likelihood-ratio terms in Equation <ref type="formula" target="#formula_2">2</ref>.

text.text: Conceptually, these values are providing estimates that each memory trace j would have been produced by some new-item-generation process.

Recall that Shiffrin and Steyvers (1997) assumed that the same geometric probability distribution produced the features of old and new test probes, which allowed them to develop their ideal-observer model.
text.formatted: Recall that <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Shiffrin and Steyvers (1997)</ref> assumed that the same geometric probability distribution produced the features of old and new test probes, which allowed them to develop their ideal-observer model.

text.text: By contrast, the specification of a new-item-generation process in the present continuous-dimension domain is more open-ended.
We formulated two candidate versions of our proposed MDS-REM model for this purpose, although a wide variety of other candidates are possible.

In the first, we imagined that the memory system assumes that all items are being randomly sampled from a single Mdimensional multivariate normal distribution with mean on each dimension m (μm) equal to the mean of all the study items on each dimension m.
For simplicity, we assumed a constant standard deviation σN on each of the dimensions of this multivariate normal and zero correlation between all pairs of dimensions.
To provide the model with some flexibility, we allowed the value of σN to be a free parameter (rather than computing it from the study items).
In addition, we needed to make provision for the probability that the new-item generation process would generate whatever distinctive feature might be possessed by memory-trace j.

The overall probability density that the new-item generation process would produce memory-trace j was therefore given by where, as before, the xjm are the values of item j on each dimension m of the MDS space; μm is the dimension-m mean of the multivariate normal that generates new items in the space (assumed here to be the mean computed across all study items); and δj is the (transformed) distinctivefeature rating for item j.
As discussed above, the multivariate-normal standard deviation σN is allowed to be a free parameter.
Finally, the value αN is a freely estimated scaling parameter that influences the magnitude of the reduction of P(Dj|Nj) that results from the distinctive feature possessed by memory-trace j.

Conceptually, Equation 6 formalizes two ideas: First, the probability density P(Dj|Nj) will tend to be small if memory-trace j lies in an isolated region of the space, because it is less likely for the new-item generation process to generate items in isolated regions.

Second, the probability density P(Dj|Nj) will tend to be small if memory-trace j possesses a highly distinctive feature, because it is less likely for the new-item generation process to generate an item with some specific highly distinctive feature.
We have now completed the presentation of the steps required for computing all the P(Dj|Sj) and P(Dj|Nj) values in the likelihood-ratio Equation 2.
text.formatted: We have now completed the presentation of the steps required for computing all the P(Dj|Sj) and P(Dj|Nj) values in the likelihood-ratio Equation <ref type="formula" target="#formula_2">2</ref>.

text.text: The final step is to use the computed likelihood-ratio (LR) value for generating a predicted probability that the test probe is judged to be old.
This probability is assumed to be given by where k is a criterion parameter; and γ is a freely estimated response-scaling parameter (e.g., Meagher & Nosofsky, 2023).
text.formatted: This probability is assumed to be given by where k is a criterion parameter; and γ is a freely estimated response-scaling parameter (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Meagher & Nosofsky, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The system tends to respond "old" when LR γ exceeds k and tends to respond "new" otherwise.
As noted above, we also formulated a second version of the MDS-REM model that assumed an alternative new-item generation process.

In brief, rather than assuming that new items were generated by sampling from a single multivariate normal, the second version integrated across the positions of the individual study items to estimate the probability that a new memory trace would be randomly generated in its respective location of the MDS space.
The fits of this second version were extremely similar to those of the first, so we present the detailed formulation of the second version in Appendix B.

Before turning to the sections of our article in which we show fits of the proposed MDS-REM model to data, it is useful to flesh out the conceptual underpinnings of the model and the types of predictions we expect it will make.
First, in general, the model will of course tend to predict that hit rates to old items will be higher than false-alarm rates to new items.

In the case of an old test probe, there will be a perfect match to a single memory trace, and here the value of P(Dj|Sj) will reach its maximum, leading to a large-magnitude LR value (see Equations 2 and 3b).
Second, lures that are highly similar to numerous memory traces will have high false-alarm rates.

In this case, even though such lures will not provide a perfect match to any given memory trace, many of the P(Dj|Sj) will be reasonably high, again leading to a relatively large-magnitude LR value (see Equations 2, 4, and 5).
Thus, we expect for example that it will successfully predict that the HSN lures will have higher false-alarm rates than the standard lures.

Third, and of greatest interest, the model potentially accounts for findings that old test probes with highly distinctive features may have elevated hit rates compared to old test probes without such features.

Under the present formulation, both types of old test probes provide a perfect match to the memory trace that they produced so will yield identical P(Dj|Sj) values with respect to their matching trace in memory (Equation 3b).
text.formatted: Under the present formulation, both types of old test probes provide a perfect match to the memory trace that they produced so will yield identical P(Dj|Sj) values with respect to their matching trace in memory (Equation <ref type="formula" target="#formula_4">3b</ref>).

text.text: In the present formulation, the key to accounting for the elevated hit rates lies in the denominator of the likelihood-ratio corresponding to the matching trace, not the numerator.

In particular, the probability that the new-item generation process will produce a memory trace with a highly distinctive feature is considerably lower than the probability that it will produce a memory trace without such a feature: the P(Dj|Nj) value will tend to be lower for high-distinctive memory traces than for low-distinctive ones (see Equation 6).
text.formatted: In particular, the probability that the new-item generation process will produce a memory trace with a highly distinctive feature is considerably lower than the probability that it will produce a memory trace without such a feature: the P(Dj|Nj) value will tend to be lower for high-distinctive memory traces than for low-distinctive ones (see Equation <ref type="formula" target="#formula_10">6</ref>).

text.text: Hence, the old/new likelihood ratio associated with the matching trace [P(Dj|Sj) /P(Dj|Nj) ] will be greater for memory traces with high distinctiveness.

If the boost in the matching-trace likelihood ratio is sufficiently large, then the summed individual-trace old/new likelihood ratios (see Equation 2) may be greater for high-distinctive old test probes than for low-distinctive ones.
text.formatted: If the boost in the matching-trace likelihood ratio is sufficiently large, then the summed individual-trace old/new likelihood ratios (see Equation <ref type="formula" target="#formula_2">2</ref>) may be greater for high-distinctive old test probes than for low-distinctive ones.

text.text: The intuition here is that the memory system is concluding that the match of a test probe to a highly distinctive memory trace provides convincing evidence that the test probe must be old because there is a very low probability that the new-item generation process would have produced such a trace by chance alone.

We should remark that, even without making special provision for the role of distinctive features, the MDS-REM model might still have the needed machinery for predicting hit rate advantages for distinctive items.

To the extent that such items lie in isolated regions of the MDS space, they will tend to yield small values of P(Dj|Nj), because their probability density in the continuous MDS space will be small in magnitude.
However, we will see that making provision for the role of distinctive features allows MDS-REM to provide considerably better accounts of the present sets of old-new recognition data.

Second, we should remark that whether MDS-REM predicts that high-distinctive items will have higher hit rates depends on the detailed structure of the MDS space in which the items are embedded and on parameter settings in the model.

Although a high-distinctive old test probe will tend to produce a large-magnitude likelihood-ratio with respect to its matching memory trace, it may produce relatively small likelihood ratios with respect to the mismatching ones, because for mismatching traces the values of P(Dj|Sj) will tend to be smaller for high-distinctive old test probes than for low-distinctive old test probes.

In short, according to the model, the presence of distinctive features in test probes exerts opposing forces on likelihood-ratio matches to traces in memory, with the final outcome being parameterdependent.

Fits to the Old-New Recognition Data of Meagher and Nosofsky (2023) We have already described the basic design of Meagher and Nosofsky's (2023) old-new recognition experiment in the context of introducing the MDS-REM model.
text.formatted: Fits to the Old-New Recognition Data of <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Meagher and Nosofsky (2023)</ref> We have already described the basic design of <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Meagher and Nosofsky's (2023)</ref> old-new recognition experiment in the context of introducing the MDS-REM model.

text.text: In this section we provide the results of fitting the model to the old-new recognition-choice data observed for each of the 540 individual items, aggregated across all participants.

We fitted the model to the data under the assumption that the "old" and "new" response frequencies for each item were binomially distributed and the frequency distributions across items were independent.
The predicted probability that an item was judged to be "old" was given by the series of MDS-REM Equations 2-7 presented in the previous section.

In the present case, use of these equations involved the estimation of 11 free parameters: the multivariate normal standard deviations σS and σN for the old and new memory-trace generation processes; the parameters γ and k in the probabilistic decision-rule (Equation 7); the three distinctive-feature scaling parameters (αT, αM, and αN) and the HSN distinctive-feature proportionality constant v; and parameters ref, p and q for transforming the distinctive feature ratings onto a psychological scale (see Appendix A).
text.formatted: In the present case, use of these equations involved the estimation of 11 free parameters: the multivariate normal standard deviations σS and σN for the old and new memory-trace generation processes; the parameters γ and k in the probabilistic decision-rule (Equation <ref type="formula" target="#formula_12">7</ref>); the three distinctive-feature scaling parameters (αT, αM, and αN) and the HSN distinctive-feature proportionality constant v; and parameters ref, p and q for transforming the distinctive feature ratings onto a psychological scale (see Appendix A).

text.text: We used the Hooke and Jeeves (1961) computer algorithm to search for the values of the free parameters that maximized the likelihood of the data and used 50 different random starting configurations in conducting the parameter searches.
text.formatted: We used the <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Hooke and Jeeves (1961)</ref> computer algorithm to search for the values of the free parameters that maximized the likelihood of the data and used 50 different random starting configurations in conducting the parameter searches.

text.text: We evaluated the overall fit of the model and some of its special cases by using the BIC statistic, given by where lnL is the natural log-likelihood of the data given the best-fitting parameters in the model, P is the number of free parameters in the model, and N is the number of observations in the data.
The model that minimizes the BIC is considered to provide the most parsimonious account of the data.
The maximum-likelihood parameters and summary fits from this full version of the model, along with some constrained special cases of the model, are reported in Table 1.
text.formatted: The maximum-likelihood parameters and summary fits from this full version of the model, along with some constrained special cases of the model, are reported in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

text.text: In Figure 1 (top panel) we display a scatterplot of the observed against MDS-REM predicted "old" recognition probabilities for each of the 540 individual items.
text.formatted: In Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">1</ref> (top panel) we display a scatterplot of the observed against MDS-REM predicted "old" recognition probabilities for each of the 540 individual items.

text.text: Although there is clearly room for improvement, in our view the model does a reasonably good job of capturing the data, especially when one considers that we are predicting recognition performance for a complex set of high-dimensional naturalistic images at the level of individual items.

As can be seen from inspection, the model captures the qualitative pattern that "old" recognition probabilities are highest for the old target items (i.e., "hits"), followed by false-alarm rates to the HSN lures, and finally false-alarm rates to the standard lures.
The model also captures to a reasonable degree the variation in false-alarm rates within the class of standard lures themselves.
Finally, it also captures much of the variability in hit rates to the individual old test probes.

Importantly, it correctly accounts for the finding that the highest hit rates tend to be associated with those old test probes that had received high distinctive-feature ratings in the independently conducted distinctive-feature rating study.
As noted in the section in which we presented the formal model, we also tested a second version of MDS-REM that posited an alternative new-item-generation process (see Appendix B for details).

As reported in Table 1, this alternative Version-2 yielded a similar BIC fit to the data as the first version and the resulting scatterplot of observed against predicted "old" recognition probabilities was extremely similar to the one already displayed.
text.formatted: As reported in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>, this alternative Version-2 yielded a similar BIC fit to the data as the first version and the resulting scatterplot of observed against predicted "old" recognition probabilities was extremely similar to the one already displayed.

text.text: It is almost certain that various of the free parameters in our current version of MDS-REM trade off with one another and that more parsimonious versions could be discovered that make use of fewer free parameters.
At its current stage of development, however, we are more interested in illustrating the promise of the modeling approach and using it as a springboard for future developments.
Thus, it seems premature to conduct computationally expensive explorations of the parameter space in a search for the most parsimonious version.
Nevertheless, here we consider some special cases of the model to investigate the role of some of its free parameters.
One question of clear interest is the extent to which the machinery involving the role of the distinctive features contributes to the model fit.

To address this question, we fitted a specialcase version of the model in which all the distinctive-feature scaling parameters (αT, αM, and αN) were held fixed at zero, such that the predictions now relied solely on the locations of the stimuli in the continuous MDS space.
As reported in Table 1, the fit of that special-case version of the model was dramatically worse than that of the full model.
text.formatted: As reported in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>, the fit of that special-case version of the model was dramatically worse than that of the full model.

text.text: The scatterplot of observed against predicted old recognition probabilities from that special-case model is shown in the bottom panel of Figure 1.
text.formatted: The scatterplot of observed against predicted old recognition probabilities from that special-case model is shown in the bottom panel of Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">1</ref>.

text.text: As can be seen, without making use of the distinctive-feature machinery, this special case version of the model provided extremely poor fits to the hit-rate data of the individual items.
It was unable to capture the magnitude of the elevated hit rates for old test probes with high distinctive-feature ratings.
A second question concerns the role of the response-scaling parameter γ in the probabilistic decision rule (Equation 7).
text.formatted: A second question concerns the role of the response-scaling parameter γ in the probabilistic decision rule (Equation <ref type="formula" target="#formula_12">7</ref>).

text.text: A special-case version of the model would set γ=1.

In our view, there is no very strong reason to assume that the response probabilities are governed by the absolute values of the likelihood ratios, so in these initial tests of the model it seemed sensible to allow γ to vary freely.

In the present application and each of our subsequent ones, the maximum-likelihood estimate of γ was less than 1, suggesting perhaps that the memory and decision system may gradually discount the likelihood-ratio evidence as it grows very large.
Nevertheless, past work has demonstrated that γ trades off with other parameters in closely related models (e.g., Krefeld-Schwalb, Pachur, & Scheibehenne, 2022; Nosofsky & Zaki, 2002).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, past work has demonstrated that γ trades off with other parameters in closely related models (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Krefeld-Schwalb, Pachur, & Scheibehenne, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Nosofsky & Zaki, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: To address this issue, we report in Table 1 the fit of the γ=1 version of the model.
text.formatted: To address this issue, we report in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> the fit of the γ=1 version of the model.

text.text: As can be seen, there is a substantial worsening of the BIC measure of fit compared to the full version of the model.
We display in an OSF supplement (mailto:https://osf.io/wpvu2) a scatterplot of the observed against predicted old-recognition probabilities from the γ=1 model.
text.formatted: We display in an OSF supplement (<ref type="url" target="mailto:https://osf.io/wpvu2">https://osf.io/wpvu2</ref>) a scatterplot of the observed against predicted old-recognition probabilities from the γ=1 model.

text.text: In brief, it produced a large gap between the highest-predicted false-alarm rates and the lowest-predicted hit rates, unlike what is seen in the observed data.
The complex computational reasons for this form of misprediction in the present paradigm remain to be investigated.
A third question involves the role of the nonlinear transform of the raw mean distinctiveness ratings onto a psychological distinctiveness scale (see Appendix A).

In our view, making allowance for such a transform is justified because there is no very strong reason to assume that the raw absolute ratings provide a valid measure of psychological distinctiveness in the context of the present modeling.
(Nevertheless, we should note that this component of the model is specific to the present application.
) In Table 1 we report the fit of a special-case version of the model in which the raw absolute mean ratings are used instead.
Again, there is a clear worsening in the BIC fit of the model.
A scatterplot of the observed against predicted oldrecognition probabilities for this special-case version of the model is provided in the OSF supplement.

Visual inspection of the scatterplot indicated that the special-case model provided a reasonably good fit to the data and succeeded at predicting that the highest hit probabilities were associated with high-distinctive targets.
However, this special-case model systematically underestimated the magnitude of that hit-rate advantage.

The best-fitting transform function from the full model (see Table 1 and Appendix A) is shown in Figure 2, and it produces low and flat measures of psychological distinctiveness for items that received low mean distinctiveness ratings, but positively accelerated measures of psychological distinctiveness for items that received high ratings.

text.text: These transformations contributed to the good fit of the model displayed in the top panel of Figure 1.

text.formatted: In their original article, <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Meagher and Nosofsky (2023)</ref> reported fits of the hybridsimilarity GCM to these same data.

text.text: As explained in greater detail in our General Discussion, the hybrid-similarity GCM is a more traditional "summed similarity" global-familiarity model rather than one that makes use of old-new likelihood ratios.

It accounts for the higher hit rates that are sometimes associated with high-distinctive items by assuming that old items with distinctive features have higher degrees of self-similarity than do items without such features.

The hybridsimilarity GCM with its distinctive-feature machinery provided roughly the same fits to the individual-item recognition data as the current MDS-REM model (see Meagher and Nosofsky, 2023, Table 4 and Figure 11).

text.text: Despite the similar fits of the models, in our view the distinctive features are contributing to the behavior of the models in somewhat conceptually different ways.
We discuss this issue at length in our General Discussion.

Fits to the Old-New Recognition Data of Nosofsky, Ehinger, and Osth (2025) In this section we report fits of the MDS-REM model to a second set of old-new recognition data, namely the data reported by Nosofsky, Ehinger, and Osth (2025).
text.formatted: Fits to the Old-New Recognition Data of <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Nosofsky, Ehinger, and Osth (2025)</ref> In this section we report fits of the MDS-REM model to a second set of old-new recognition data, namely the data reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Nosofsky, Ehinger, and Osth (2025)</ref>.

text.text: The purpose of that study was to provide tests of the hybrid-similarity GCM's ability to account jointly for the effects of distinctive features, category size, and within-and between-category similarity on oldnew recognition data.
In their experiment, the stimulus set was composed of a set of rock images organized into 24 categories with 10 items per category.
As in the Meagher and Nosofsky (2023) project, an MDS study was conducted to embed the individual images in a similarity space with 8 dimensions.
text.formatted: As in the <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Meagher and Nosofsky (2023)</ref> project, an MDS study was conducted to embed the individual images in a similarity space with 8 dimensions.

text.text: In addition, distinctive-feature ratings for all items were collected from a separate group of participants.
In the old-new recognition experiment itself, each observer was presented with a unique study list in which the 24 categories were randomly assigned to different size conditions.
The study list had five size-1 categories, five size-2, five size-4 and five size-8 categories.
In addition, there were four size-0 categories that did not appear on the study list.
The images that served as study items from each category were randomly chosen for each individual participant.
Following the study phase, observers were presented with two old target items and two new lure items from each of the categories and judged whether each item was old or new.
(Only a single target was available for the size-1 categories.
The items that served as targets and lures during the test phase were again randomly sampled for each individual observer.)

The general pattern of results was that: i) false-alarm rates increased systematically with increases in category size; ii) hit rates showed a smaller increase with increases in category size; iii) false-alarm rates were greater for categories with higher within-category similarity than for categories with lower within-category similarity; iv) hit rates tended to be higher for items composed of high-distinctive features; and v) false-alarm rates were reduced for items composed of high-distinctive features.
The hybrid-similarity GCM provided a reasonably good simultaneous account of all these qualitative effects.
It is straightforward to apply MDS-REM to the data from this study.

The model is defined by the same system of equations as in the previous section; however, because Nosofsky et al. (2025) did not include the HSN manipulation that had been used by Meagher and Nosofsky (2023), we no longer need to make special provision for HSN lures.

text.text: As can been, there was a systematic increase in false-alarm rates as category size increased and a smaller increase in hit rates.
The full version of MDS-REM does a good job of capturing the effects, although it slightly underestimates the magnitude of the increase in false alarms.
The model predicts the category-size effect on false alarms because the larger is category size, the greater is the number of memory traces with high similarity to the tested lures.
Thus, the summed likelihood-ratio similarity tends to increase, resulting in higher probabilities of "old" responses.

Increases in category size have a smaller impact on the hit rates, because the similarity of the old test probe to its own memory trace dominates the sum, with the interitem similarities exerting smaller relative effects.

As can be seen in the bottom panel of Figure 3, the special-case version of MDS-REM without distinctive-feature scaling predicts similar qualitative effects, but it significantly underestimates the absolute magnitude of the hit rates.
text.formatted: As can be seen in the bottom panel of Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3</ref>, the special-case version of MDS-REM without distinctive-feature scaling predicts similar qualitative effects, but it significantly underestimates the absolute magnitude of the hit rates.

text.text: A likely reason is that without making provision for the role of the distinctive features, it fails to properly estimate the small magnitude of the P(Dj|Nj) terms in the denominators of the individual-trace likelihood ratios, so underestimates the summed likelihood-ratio similarity for the old test probes.

Figure 4 plots the mean observed and MDS-REM predicted false-alarm and hit rates for each of the individual 24 categories (e.g., granite, marble, sandstone, etc.) averaged across the different size conditions.

text.text: The model does a good job overall of capturing these individualcategory effects.

In general, it predicts higher false-alarm rates for categories with higher degrees of within-category similarity: As within-category similarity increases, the magnitudes of the P(Dj|Sj) terms in the numerators of the memory-trace likelihood ratios tend to increase, so the model predicts higher probabilities of responding "old".
More interesting, it also does a good job of predicting the mean hit rates across the 24 individual categories.
The most likely explanation is that some categories tend to have more members with highly distinctive features.

In these cases, the denominator of the likelihood-ratio term corresponding to the memory trace that was produced by the old test item tends to be small in magnitude; thus, the old/new likelihood ratio for the matching trace is large and the memory system correctly judges the test probe to be old.

Some confirming evidence for this explanation can be found in the lower-panel In Figure 5 we provide plots of the observed against model-predicted hit-minus-falsealarm rates, which provide a rough measure of the extent to which observers were able to discriminate between old versus new test probes of each of the categories.

Although the special-case version without the distinctivefeature scaling parameters yields predictions that are highly correlated with the observed data, its absolute fit to these data is poor, because it systematically under-predicts performance.

text.text: Hence, we needed to rely on various approximation assumptions regarding the structure of the stimulus sets to implement the proposed model.

In this section, we instead apply the model to results from an experimental paradigm in which the full stimulus structure is known, namely the Nosofsky and Zaki (2003) old-new recognition paradigm in which the hybrid-similarity GCM was originally formalized and tested.

Thus, this illustration should be regarded as a "proof-ofconcept" of how MDS-REM can be applied in cases in which the distinctive features are known instead of approximated from ratings.
In Nosofsky and Zaki's Experiment-2 conditions, the stimuli were Munsell color patches drawn from a set of 6 highly separated hue regions.
Within each hue region, the configuration of stimuli was as illustrated in Figure 7.

For each participant, three items from each circular ring of each hue region were randomly selected to serve as study items; the remaining half of the circular-ring items as well as the prototypes served as foils.
In addition, half of the hue regions were randomly selected to serve as "marked" regions.

We adapted the MDS-REM model in a straightforward way to account for the observed pattern of recognition data in this paradigm.

Note that there was a total of 18 study items (3 study items from each of the 6 hue regions); thus, for all item types presented during the test phase, the LR equations will involve an average across 18 likelihood-ratios associated with each of the memory traces.

Because the different hue regions were so widely separated, we assume a minuscule contribution of between-hue-region confusions among the items; for simplicity, we define a parameter b as the between-hue-region probability density that test item i gives rise to memory-trace j and set b=.001.
Unlike in our previous applications, the distinctive features of the objects are known, so we no longer need to rely on separate sets of distinctive-feature ratings for the items.

We assume for simplicity that the magnitude of the distinctive-feature mismatches are the same for each of the distinctive features that were used and without loss of generality we can set the magnitude of the mismatches at δ=1.
The remaining parameters for computing the numerators of the individual-trace likelihood-ratio values [i.e., the values of P(Dj|Sj)] are the same as defined in the previous sections of our article.
So, for example, consider the case of the distinctive-old (DO) items.

text.text: Next, we need to specify the values of P(Dj|Nj) for each type of memory trace, i.e., the probability density that a new-item-generation process would have given rise to each memory trace.

Given the structure of the stimulus set in this paradigm, in which each coordinate is roughly equally likely by design, a simple approximation was to assume a constant uniform probability density u that each memory trace in the continuous space would be produced by that process: new foils because the old targets produce elevated values of P(Dj|Sj) in the numerator of the likelihood-ratios in the case in which they are compared to their own trace in memory.

Foils that are more similar on average to these memory traces produce higher false-alarm rates for the same type of reason, accounting for the finding that the prototype foils had higher false-alarm rates than the standard foils.
The results for the HSDF and LSDF distinctive foils are instructive.
The HSDF and LSDF foils both have a distinctive feature that matches the distinctive feature of a DO study item.
However, only the HSDF foil lies in the same hue region as that DO study item.
There is a very low probability that the LSDF item could have produced the DO memory trace with a completely different hue, accounting for its very low false-alarm rate.
Interestingly, the false-alarm rate for the HSDF foil is lower in magnitude than for the TF foils, a result that is also correctly accounted for by the model.

Although the HSDF foil provides a better match than the TF foils to the DO study item in its hue region (because it matches the DO study item on its distinctive feature), it provides a worse match to the TO study items.
Averaged across all study items, the averaged old/new likelihood-ratio turns out to be greater for the TF foils than for the HSDF foil.

In past work in other domains, it has sometimes been observed that foils with very high similarity to a specific old target are endorsed with lower probability than are typical foils, and this pattern of results has been taken as evidence for a "recall-to-reject" process that operates in concert with a global familiarity-based process (for a review and integrated theory, see Malmberg, 2008).

text.text: It is interesting to note that here we are illustrating a specific case in which a global-familiarity-only model successfully accounts for such a pattern of results.

Clearly, however, the predicted pattern of results from MDS-REM will be highly dependent on the detailed structure of the MDS space in which the items are embedded and on parameter settings in the model.
In the limit, if the HSDF foil were made arbitrarily similar to the DO study item, its false alarm rate would be the same as the hit rate for the DO item itself.

Future work should pursue similar directions using richer sets of real-world multidimensional stimuli.

Although MDS-REM substitutes a continuous probability-density function for the discrete geometric function used in original REM, and also makes special provision for the role of distinctive features, the intent was to preserve the basic spirit and conceptions of original REM.

It is an open question, however, the extent to which MDS-REM can reproduce many of the same qualitative predictions of fundamental memory phenomena to which original REM has been successfully applied.
Given the enormous number of effects that have been studied in the past literature, a comprehensive investigation of this question goes beyond the scope of the present article.
Nevertheless, in this final section, we begin the investigation by examining two major phenomena, namely the list-length effect and the mirror effect for high-frequency vs. lowfrequency words.

For simplicity in these preliminary investigations, we dispense with the component of the model that makes provision for the role of distinctive features and focus on the question of whether the use of continuous-dimension representations of objects produces similar predictions as use of the discrete geometric-feature probability function.
A robust phenomenon is that as list length increases, observers' ability to discriminate between old target items and novel lures decreases.
Moreover, the results often show a mirror effect: as list length increases, the probability of hits decreases, whereas the probability of false alarms increases (e.g., Murnane & Shiffrin, 1991).
text.formatted: Moreover, the results often show a mirror effect: as list length increases, the probability of hits decreases, whereas the probability of false alarms increases (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Murnane & Shiffrin, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: To simulate this experimental manipulation, we constructed randomly-generated items varying along 8 dimensions (matching the MDS solutions for the rock-image experiments analyzed earlier in this article).

Old study instances and novel lures were both drawn from an identical multivariate normal distribution with mean zero along each dimension, standard deviation σ along each dimension, and with zero correlation between all pairs of dimensions.
As in our previous applications, we assumed for simplicity that the generated items were stored in an error-free manner in memory.
We assumed that the memory system was able to form a good estimate of the standard deviation σ that was used in the item-generation process.
Thus, the memory system's estimate of the probability that a new-item-generation process would produce each memory trace was given by
For simplicity in the simulations, we set σ=1.
As in the rock-image experiments, the probability density that each memory trace j was produced during the study phase by a given test item i was assumed to be given by
It is an open question how the memory system would produce an estimate of σs; for simplicity, in the present simulation, we again set σs = σ = 1.

For each test item, the averaged likelihood-ratio across all memory traces was then given by Equation 2, and the predicted probability that the test item was judged to be "old" was then given by the Equation-7 probabilistic-response rule.

text.text: We conducted 10,000 simulations of the above process for study-list lengths equal to 4, 10, 20, 40, and 80.
In each simulation, there was an equal number of old study items and new lures presented during test.
Averaged across the 10,000 simulations, the mean probabilities of hits and false alarms as a function of list length are displayed in Figure 8.
text.formatted: Averaged across the 10,000 simulations, the mean probabilities of hits and false alarms as a function of list length are displayed in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_12">8</ref>.

text.text: It is evident from inspection that the model produces the fundamental list-length effect, with hits steadily decreasing as a function of list length and false alarms steadily increasing.
The same qualitative pattern of results arises across a wide range of parameter settings in the model simulations.

The model predicts decreasing probabilities of hits as list length increases because the high likelihood-ratio for the matching trace is diluted by averaging it together with an increasing number of lower likelihood-ratios for mismatching traces.

The model predicts increasing falsealarm rates because as list length increases, there is an increased probability that study instances with high similarity to a test lure will be produced by chance alone.
It should be noted that more recent work has indicated that increases in list-length do not necessarily produce a mirror effect (Fox, Dennis, & Osth, 2020; Yim, Dennis, & Osth, 2025).
text.formatted: It should be noted that more recent work has indicated that increases in list-length do not necessarily produce a mirror effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Fox, Dennis, & Osth, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Yim, Dennis, & Osth, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, longer lists often do not necessarily show decreased hit rates but do show much larger false alarm rates.

Our intention here is to not necessarily argue that MDS-REM shows the "ideal" predictions for list length in recognition memory, but rather to demonstrate that it shows similar predictions as the original REM model.

It also should be noted that both MDS-REM as well as the original REM model may be able to "break" the mirror effect predictions for list length by allowing different response criteria for each list length condition.

Stimulus Mirror Effects. Glanzer and Adams (1985, 1990) documented a number of stimulus-related manipulations that produce mirror effects and emphasized their theoretical relevance for models of recognition memory, such as word frequency, concreteness, and pictures vs. words.
text.formatted: Stimulus Mirror Effects. <ref type="bibr">Glanzer and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Adams (1985, 1990)</ref> documented a number of stimulus-related manipulations that produce mirror effects and emphasized their theoretical relevance for models of recognition memory, such as word frequency, concreteness, and pictures vs. words.

text.text: The most common target for models of recognition memory is the word-frequency mirror effect, in which low frequency words exhibit higher hit rates and lower false alarm rates than high frequency words.

The original version of REM accounts for this finding not because low-frequency words have lower base rates than high-frequency words; rather, the key to accounting for the effect is REM's assumption that the features that compose low-frequency words tend to be rarer than those that compose high-frequency words (Cox & Shiffrin, 2017; Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997).
