text.text: We discuss that idea in more detail below in terms of MDS-REM simulations.
As in our simulations of the list-length effect, we generated simulated items by making random draws from a multivariate normal distribution.
While our approach is general and can in principle apply to any stimulus-related mirror effect, we discuss it here with reference to the word-frequency mirror effect.
Analogues of "high-frequency" words were generated by setting σ=1, whereas analogues of "low-frequency" words were generated by setting σ=1.5.
Thus, the dimension values of low-frequency words tended to be rarer (i.e., arise with lower probability) than those of high-frequency words.

We illustrated reasonably successful application of the proposed model across three previously published sets of old-new recognition data that examined performance either at the level of individual items or individual categories of items.

The model did reasonably well at predicting: 1) variations in both false-alarm and hit rates associated with individual items sampled from a real-world category domain; 2) the role of distinctiveness in elevating individual-item hit rates from this domain; 3) systematic increases in false-alarm rates with increases in category size; 4) smaller increases in hit rates with increases in category size; 4) the joint roles of distinctiveness and category structure on both false-alarm and hit rates and on overall category discriminability; 5) and how hit and false-alarm rates for individual item types varied with explicit manipulations of similarity structure and presence of distinctive features in a paradigm using highly controlled multidimensional stimuli.

Furthermore, in preliminary investigations, we showed that the model also seems to produce the same types of qualitative predictions of fundamental memory phenomena as original REM, for much the same reasons as in original REM.
Although there is still clearly room for improvement, we consider the proposed ideas to be highly promising and deserving of continued exploration and testing.

In past work, Nosofsky et al. (2019 Nosofsky et al. ( , 2020) ) acknowledged that the MDS solution derived for the rock stimuli provided only an approximation to the detailed similarity structure of this complex set of real-world, high-dimensional images.

(2020) found evidence, for example, that in tasks of classification learning, observers were sensitive to some "supplementary" dimensions of the rock stimuli that were highly diagnostic of category category old-new recognition supports that hypothesis, but future work is needed to provide a more comprehensive evaluation.

In formulating MDS-REM, we borrowed certain ideas formalized within the hybridsimilarity GCM (Meagher & Nosofsky, 2023; Nosofsky, et al., 2025; Nosofsky & Zaki, 2003), which also uses information about the location of individual items in MDS spaces as well as the distinctive features possessed by the individual items.
text.formatted: In formulating MDS-REM, we borrowed certain ideas formalized within the hybridsimilarity GCM <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Meagher & Nosofsky, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Nosofsky, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Nosofsky & Zaki, 2003)</ref>, which also uses information about the location of individual items in MDS spaces as well as the distinctive features possessed by the individual items.

text.text: The current version of MDS-REM provides similar fits as does the hybrid-similarity GCM to the sets of old-new recognition data considered in the present article.
Nevertheless, in our view, there seems to be a conceptual difference in the manner in which the models operate.

According to the hybrid-similarity GCM, the reason why items with highly distinctive features often have higher hit rates than do items without such features is that items with high distinctiveness have a greater degree of selfsimilarity to their traces in memory than do items without such features (cf., Tversky, 1977).
text.formatted: According to the hybrid-similarity GCM, the reason why items with highly distinctive features often have higher hit rates than do items without such features is that items with high distinctiveness have a greater degree of selfsimilarity to their traces in memory than do items without such features (cf., <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Tversky, 1977)</ref>.

text.text: This increased degree of self-match increases the magnitude of the overall global-familiarity signal, leading to higher hit rates for items with highly distinctive features.

By contrast, if one thinks of self-similarity in terms of the numerators of the individual-trace likelihood-ratios in MDS-REM [i.e., the P(Dj|Sj) terms], which compute the probability that a study item would have given rise to a particular memory trace, then the present version of MDS-REM conceptualizes self-similarity as being identical for items with and without distinctive features.
Instead, MDS-REM accounts for the higher hit rates associated with such items because the denominator of the likelihood ratio [i.e., the P(Dj|Nj) factor) is reduced for such items.

As discussed earlier in our article, it is as if the memory system is reasoning that there is a very low probability that the new-item generation process would have produced such a trace by chance alone; therefore, the match of a test probe to a highly distinctive memory trace provides convincing evidence that the test probe must be old.
We acknowledge that what we have characterized above as a conceptual difference may simply reflect different ways of describing the same core principles.
Indeed, MDS-REM and the hybrid-similarity GCM behave similarly in another important respect as well.

Although the presence of distinctive features in a study item tends to boost its "match" to its own memory trace (either by increasing the old/new likelihood ratio or by increasing self-similarity), it tends to reduce its interitem similarity to all non-matching traces.
(In the hybrid-similarity GCM, the equation for computing the similarity of a test item to a non-matching trace is extremely similar to what is formalized in Equation 4for MDS-REM.)
text.formatted: (In the hybrid-similarity GCM, the equation for computing the similarity of a test item to a non-matching trace is extremely similar to what is formalized in Equation <ref type="formula" target="#formula_6">4</ref>for MDS-REM.)

text.text: Thus, both models posit that the presence of distinctive features in old test probes tends to exert opposing forces on memory: increases in the self-match to the probe's own memory trace but decreases in interitem similarity to all nonmatching traces.
The prediction that there will be elevated hit rates for test probes with distinctive features holds only if the boost to the self-match exceeds the reduction to the summed interitem similarities.
For both models, such a prediction is therefore highly dependent on the detailed structure of the MDS space in which the items are embedded and on parameter settings in the models.
Perhaps the main take-home message should be that the converging predictions from the models reinforce more strongly core general principles that both models are intended to formalize.

Finally, we should point out relations between the present proposed modeling approach and ideas advanced recently by Cox (2026), who proposed an approach for transforming machine-learning representations of complex objects into likelihood-based measures of pairwise similarity.
text.formatted: Finally, we should point out relations between the present proposed modeling approach and ideas advanced recently by <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Cox (2026)</ref>, who proposed an approach for transforming machine-learning representations of complex objects into likelihood-based measures of pairwise similarity.

text.text: Modern machine-learning models produce high-dimensional vectors of features for the representation of complex objects such as words and images.
A common method for measuring the similarity between any two vector representations is to compute the cosine of the angle between them.

Cox proposes a further theoretically-motivated operation in which the cosine similarity is transformed into a ratio of the relative likelihood that the two representations code the same versus different items.
This likelihood-ratio measure of similarity can then be "plugged in" to a variety of cognitive models, such as drift-diffusion models, for generating

The major difference between MDS-REM and original REM lies in MDS-REM's use of representations corresponding to individual items lying in multidimensional similarity spaces and its associated use of continuous probability density functions rather than simulations from a hypothetical geometric-feature probability distribution.

However, a second difference involves where we placed the noise in the system: rather than assuming noisy storage and use of a deterministic decision rule (as in original REM), in implementing MDS-REM we assumed errorfree storage and use of a probabilistic decision rule.
We used the latter approach solely for reasons of facilitating computations and avoiding the need for time-consuming computer simulations.

It is straightforward to translate the present approach by allowing for noisy storage of the study items in the continuous MDS similarity space and implementing a deterministic decision rule when making old-new judgments.
On any given simulation of noisy storage of the study items, the system would respond "old" if the averaged individual old/new trace likelihoods exceeded a criterion k, and respond "new" otherwise.
The overall predictions of old/new probabilities for the individual items would be derived by averaging across multiple simulations of noisy storage.
Cox (2026) explicitly compared REM-like models both with and without the assumption of encoding variability and found support for its presence.
Future research is needed to examine versions of MDS-REM that incorporate the assumption of noisy storage and encoding variability of the memory traces.

The MDS-REM model we propose is relevant to research on individual item "memorability", namely the finding that individual items systematically differ from each other in their hit and false alarm rates (Bainbridge, 2019; Dubey et al., 2015; Kramer, Hebart, et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The MDS-REM model we propose is relevant to research on individual item "memorability", namely the finding that individual items systematically differ from each other in their hit and false alarm rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bainbridge, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Dubey et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Kramer, Hebart, et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The dominant interpretation in this literature is that variations in item memorability are intrinsic to the items themselves, which stems from the fact that individual participants show strong consistencies in terms of the studied items they recognize as well as the nonstudied items they falsely recognize.
Global familiarity models like the MDS-REM model we present in this article offer an alternative interpretation of these results.
According to this class of models, there are no features that inherently make an item memorable or non-memorable.
Instead, a stimulus is endorsed as "old" when there is a strong match between its features and the contents of memory.

For instance, in the absence of highly distinctive features, an item that is in a dense region of the MDS space is likely to yield a relatively high hit rate if it is tested as a target or a relatively high false alarm rate if it is tested as a lure.

For this reason, the systematic variations in memorability among items instead stem from a consistency in the experimental context -stimuli that tend to come from dense regions in an MDS space will also tend to be accompanied by other similar items on a given study list even if the items are randomly sampled from the set of all possible items (Simpson, Wixted, & Brady, 2026).
text.formatted: For this reason, the systematic variations in memorability among items instead stem from a consistency in the experimental context -stimuli that tend to come from dense regions in an MDS space will also tend to be accompanied by other similar items on a given study list even if the items are randomly sampled from the set of all possible items <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Simpson, Wixted, & Brady, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The MDS-REM model we propose makes this goal considerably more feasible and offers some new insights into understanding memorability.

According to MDS-REM, memorability is a joint function of the detailed similarity between a test item and the contents of memory as well as how consistent the item is with a new-item generation process.

text.text: From inspection of the figure, it is clear that the mean hit rates systematically increased as the distinctive-feature ratings increased, whereas the false-alarm rates decreased.
The full version of MDS-REM provides a good quantitative account of the pattern of results.

For old test probes with high distinctiveness, the denominator of the likelihood-ratio term [P(Dj|Nj)] associated with the matching memory trace is small, so the overall old/new likelihood-ratio associated with the matching trace is large, yielding a high hit rate.
By contrast, the special-case MDS-REM without the distinctive-feature scaling parameters fails to predict the increase in the hit rates.

text.text: As can be seen, the model produces the mirror effect, in which low-frequency items have higher hit rates and lower false-alarm rates than do high-frequency items.
The same qualitative pattern of results is again produced across a wide range of parameter settings in the model.

The low-frequency hit-rate advantage arises because the probability-density that the new-item generation process would produce a low-frequency memory trace is lower than the probability that it would produce a high-frequency memory trace --i.e., the denominator of the likelihood ratio for the matching trace is smaller for low-frequency items than for high-frequency ones.

The lower false-alarm rates for low-frequency lures arise because low-frequency lures tend to have lower similarity to old study instances than do highfrequency lures: the low-frequency lures tend to lie in more isolated regions of the similarity space.

In sum, these preliminary simulation investigations show promise that MDS-REM will produce similar qualitative predictions of fundamental memory phenomena as original REM, for very much the same reasons.
Future research is needed, however, to examine its predictions across the vast array of different memory phenomena to which original REM has been successfully applied.

text.text: Hence, a likely route to improving the detailed quantitative predictions from MDS-REM would involve the derivation of an improved MDS solution.

Even using the present MDS solution, higher-parameter versions of MDS-REM that make allowance for dimensional attention weighting (e.g., Nosofsky, 1991) and/or correlations between dimensions (e.g., Ashby & Perrin, 1988) could likely provide still more accurate quantitative accounts of the data (e.g., see Meagher & Nosofsky, 2023).

text.text: Here our focus was on demonstrating that even a low-parameter version of the model was capable of yielding quite reasonable predictions of oldnew recognition performance at the level of individual items or categories in a complex realworld domain.
Future research is needed to investigate the extent to which improved MDS solutions and higher-parameters versions of the model would improve upon the results reported thus far.

We should emphasize, however, that even with improved MDS solutions, we believe that the distinctive-feature machinery that is part of MDS-REM will continue to play a major role in the model's operation.

To reiterate the conceptual development from our introduction, there seem to be situations in which objects possess features that "stand outside" a continuousdimension geometric space in which most of the other objects are embedded.

In the domain of human faces, an occasional instance may possess a highly prominent scar or a black eye; in a domain such as animals, an occasional instance may possess two tails; and in the present rocks domain, an occasional instance may possess a fossil or a prominent crystal.

The MDS-REM equations formalize the hypothesis that such distinctive features are likely to exert a fundamental influence on old-new recognition performance that is not easily captured in terms of continuous, low-dimensional MDS solutions.

Appendix A

Transformation of Mean Distinctive-Feature Ratings onto a Psychological Scale Following Meagher and Nosofsky (2023), we used the following functions to transform the mean distinctive-feature ratings into measures of psychological distinctiveness.
First, we defined a parameter ref that denoted a "reference" value on the rating scale.

For any mean rating δ(i)' that exceeded ref, we set δ(i) = ref + (δ(i)' -ref) p and for any δ(i)' less than or equal to ref, we set δ(i) = ref -(ref -δ(i)') q where ref, p and q are freely estimated parameters.
Note that for the special case p = q = 1, δ(i) = δ(i)'.

The parameters p, q and ref make allowance for nonlinear relations between psychological distinctiveness and the direct ratings, with the allowance that the shape of the nonlinear relation differs to the left and right of the reference value.

text.text: REM model and its extensions have provided comprehensive and elegant accounts of extremely wide varieties of fundamental memory phenomena.

Nevertheless, a limitation of extant versions of the model is that they do not allow for predictions of old-new recognition performance at the level of individual items based on the items' precise locations in multidimensional similarity space and the presence of item-specific distinctive features.
To move in the direction of filling this gap, in this work we proposed a REM-like model that incorporates such information.

Our proposed MDS-REM model retains the core conceptual ideas formalized in original REM in which the memory system computes likelihood ratios that individual memory traces were produced by study items versus a new-item generation process.
